I am 68 years old. My back aches when the weather turns, but my hands still remember how to sow a straight row. I have farmed these 16.1 mu for 35 years, since I was 33. My household has seven mouths, and my son and his wife work in a factory in the city, so it is mostly me, my wife, and my daughter-in-law when she is home. We have a well, which means I do not fear drought as much as some neighbors.

Cotton is my main crop and my livelihood. This year I will plant 13 mu with cotton, as I always do. I will buy improved seeds from the county supply station—the kinds I know, like the ones they call guoxinmian or lumianyan. I do not trust strange new names. In late April, when the soil warms, I will rotary till and sow. For fertilizer, I will put down compound fertilizer as a base and top-dress with urea at flowering. I figure about 18 kg of nitrogen, 6 kg of phosphorus, and 8 kg of potassium per mu—enough to feed the plants without wasting money. I will irrigate three times from my well: once after sowing if the rain fails, once in July when the flowers set, and once in August when the bolls are filling. I will spray pesticide ten times. The bollworm never sleeps, and I walk my fields every morning to check the leaves. If the weather is fair, I expect 550 kg of seed cotton per mu.

The remaining 3.1 mu I keep for stevia. A buyer from the processing plant pays a steady price, and that cash covers my grandson's school fees. I will plant improved stevia seedlings in early April, rotary till the plot, and lay ridges so water does not sit at the roots. Stevia needs less feed than cotton—about 14 kg nitrogen, 5 kg phosphorus, and 8 kg potassium per mu. It likes moisture but not wet feet, so I will irrigate four times carefully. I spray six times because aphids love the tender leaves. I expect about 550 kg of fresh leaves per mu.

That is my plan. I do not change what works.
